Instead, he pointed to a form of “communal property” and to a particular mode associated with it, connected in some way with communal ownership.
Marx located this historical form “among the Indians, the Slavs, the ancient Celts, and so on.”
This example, together with similar remarks Marx made on several occasions, later became widely associated with what was called the Asiatic mode of production.
The letters exchanged between Marx and Engels about forms of property in Eastern societies cast further light on this question.
In one of these letters, Marx wrote to Engels that he agreed with Bernier’s view that the key to understanding the phenomena of the East was the absence of private ownership of land.
“This,” Marx wrote, “is the real key even to the Eastern paradise.”
Engels replied that the absence of private ownership of land was indeed, in a deeper sense, the key to the whole East and the basis of its political and religious history.
But why, he asked, did Eastern peoples not develop private ownership of land, even in a feudal form?

Engels answered that the main reason lay in the natural climate and character of the land, especially the vast desert regions stretching from the Sahara in North Africa through Arabia, Persia and India and into the highlands of Asia and Tartary—what is now Soviet Central Asia and part of Turkestan.
Artificial irrigation, he argued, was the first condition of agriculture in these regions. Irrigation had to be organized either by the communal group, by the region, or by the central government.

Governments in the East, Engels wrote, traditionally had three main functions: finance, meaning the extraction of wealth from their own country; war, meaning the plunder of their own country and neighbouring countries; and public works (Travaux Publics), which were necessary to increase production.

The British government, he said, organized the first two functions and gave them an even more cunning form, while completely abolishing the third. The result was the destruction of agriculture in India.
Free competition was useless under these conditions.
The fertility of the land depended on artificial irrigation, and disappeared as soon as the irrigation system collapsed.

This, Engels argued, explains something that would otherwise be difficult to understand: whole regions that had once been magnificently cultivated later became abandoned deserts. He mentioned Palmyra, Petra, the ruins of Yemen, and many areas of Egypt, Persia and India.
It also explains, he said, how a single destructive war could empty a country of its population and destroy its civilization for centuries.

“In my view, the collapse of trade in southern Arabia in the period before Muḥammad—which you rightly regard as one of the most important factors behind the Islamic revolution—belongs to exactly this kind of phenomenon.”

Texts like these show that the founders of Marxism did not close the door of scientific inquiry to any historical experience. They were prepared to take new evidence into account when applying Marxist theories, based on the general objective laws of social development, to concrete historical conditions.

Among later and contemporary Marxists—and especially Soviet Orientalists and researchers—there was no single agreed picture of social relations in the Arabian Peninsula during the fifth and sixth centuries CE and at the time Islam first appeared.

We believe the main reason is that the historical evidence for this period of Arab history is not rich enough to allow modern researchers to reconstruct a complete and realistic picture of its actual economic and social relations.

This shortage of evidence comes above all from the methods used by the Arab historians who lived closest to the period. They often devoted great attention to secondary details that tell us very little about the underlying social reality.

Modern researchers, especially those who do not read Arabic sources directly, have therefore often had to rely on works written long after the earliest Islamic centuries, such as al-Shahrastānī’s famous Religions and Sects, or on the writings of modern travellers and later researchers.

These works look back at the older reality from a distance of more than fourteen centuries. They can therefore reconstruct it only indirectly, from the surviving remains of the distant past and from earlier written sources that are themselves incomplete.
The Russian-Soviet Orientalist Ignatius Krachkovsky, who had an exceptionally broad knowledge of Arabic studies, relied more heavily on pre-Islamic poetry.

He treated it as “the oldest surviving monument of the Arabic language,” and therefore, for the history of that period, as “not only the oldest source but in truth the only surviving source we have for the events it describes.”
Krachkovsky therefore believed that pre-Islamic poetry gives us a faithful picture of Arab tribal life as a whole.

He rejected the various theories questioning whether this poetry genuinely belonged to the pre-Islamic period, because he did not believe there was decisive evidence for doubting its value as a historical source for the study of pre-Islamic Arabia.
Soviet historical studies contain several different views about the particular character of economic and social relations in the late pre-Islamic period.
The Soviet Orientalist Yevgeny Belyaev, author of The Arabs, Islam and the Arab Caliphate, discusses several of these theories.

One is what he calls the “commercial-capitalist” theory, which he attributes to Reisnev. Belyaev says that this theory was widespread in the 1920s and 1930s and that it “differs sharply from Marxist-Leninist theory.”
He also discusses a “stage theory” and an “agrarian theory.”
The first argues that the rise of Islam “reflected and embodied the interests and ideals of the Bedouin tribes of Arabia.”
The second argues that Islam first arose as “an expression of the aspirations of the landless class.”
Belyaev rejects both theories because, in his view, “neither has any scientific basis.”

He then refers to a study by S. P. Tolstov on the origins of Islam. Tolstov paid particular attention to slavery in the Arabian Peninsula during the fifth and sixth centuries CE. Belyaev describes his work as a deep historical study supported by evidence and argument.
Another theory argues that “Islam first arose as the ideology of early feudal society.”
The Russian Orientalists A. Yu. Yakubovsky and I. P. Petrushevsky reject this feudal interpretation, however, and instead stress slavery in Arabia, its origins and its development.

Belyaev also praises the scientific value of what he calls the “deep study supported by convincing arguments” found in the third volume of the large Soviet work History of the World, published in Moscow in 1957. He says that it presents “the essential historical events and developments taking place in Arabia during the fifth and sixth centuries, including those connected with the first emergence of Islam.”
Belyaev’s own position can be summarized as follows:

The population of the Arabian Peninsula was a mixture of nomadic Bedouins and settled communities living mainly from agriculture. Marx’s observation applies here: “From the beginning of recorded history, we find in the East a connection between settled urban life among one part of the population and nomadic life among another.”

During the fifth and sixth centuries CE, most of the population of Arabia—with the exception of the settled population of Yemen—still lived within a primitive form of social organization. Society had not yet divided into clearly defined social classes, and there was no state or developed system of government.
The dominant structure was that of tribe and clan, based primarily on blood ties and descent, but also on forms of “brotherhood” that allowed outsiders to join a clan through political alliance.

At the same time, however, differences in wealth were becoming greater. Private ownership of livestock already existed, developing earlier than private ownership of land, and slaves were used both in herding and in agriculture.
As inequality in the distribution of wealth grew, it created the material basis for the first signs of breakdown in the tribal economic and social order that had existed before the rise of classes.
The power of clans and their leaders rested increasingly on wealth and economic position rather than simply on custom or social prestige.

Belyaev also argues that the level of development reached by Arabian society during this period—again excluding Yemen—corresponded to what Engels described as the stage before the full emergence of class society, when “human beings begin to use iron for their tools and implements, then move toward civilization with the invention of alphabetic writing.”

The Arabs of the Jāhiliyya had, in his view, reached this stage. Society had developed groups of craftsmen and farmers. Pottery was made, textiles were woven, smelted metals were used, swords and iron ploughs were produced, and gold and silver were worked.

By the time Islam appeared, trade and lending at interest were helping to break down tribal relations and weaken the old order, because a tribal system could not easily coexist with an economy increasingly based on money.
The wealth of the Quraysh leaders included money, trade, farms, slaves and livestock.

In Mecca, Medina and Ṭāʾif there were workers involved in obtaining and handling goods, as well as workers outside the traditional crafts who performed many other kinds of labour, including veterinary work, herding livestock and watering camels used in trade caravans.

The breakdown of the old communal tribal system, which happened earlier in Mecca than elsewhere, brought the clans of Quraysh into a new form of organization. A group of leading notables now dominated political life through simple formal institutions used to manage clan affairs, including the malaʾ, or council of notables, and Dār al-Nadwa, the assembly house.

By the end of the Jāhiliyya, paganism was also reaching the end of its historical life. New class relations were entering the old tribal communal order, helping produce a shift away from polytheism and toward monotheism.

Alliances between tribes reflected a growing desire to unite Arabia and create a central authority. Such unity, in Belyaev’s view, required a monotheistic belief that people would respect and hold sacred.
It was in this setting that Ḥanīfiyya, a form of Arab monotheism, appeared.

Yet Ḥanīfiyya did not spread widely in Mecca. This was not only because the Quraysh opposed it, but also because of the social conditions inside the city: the conflicts between merchants and moneylenders on one side and those harmed by usury on the other, and between slave owners and slaves who wanted freedom.
Ḥanīfiyya did not originally express the aspirations of these oppressed groups. At first, its preaching went little beyond the idea that worldly life is temporary.
But as Meccan society developed, Ḥanīfiyya developed with it and eventually entered a stage in which it helped prepare the ground for Islam.

Belyaev’s final conclusion is that Islam arose in Arabia as a new ideology reflecting the major changes taking place in Arab society: growing inequality in the distribution of wealth, slavery and expanding commercial exchange.
With Islam came a new form of organization: the “community of believers.”
This new community directly contradicted the old tribal system. It became the basic social foundation on which the Islamic state was built.
Belyaev sees this as confirming the theory that “the first attempt to establish a state must involve destroying the tribal organization and breaking apart its structure.”

When we turn to the historical form of the mode of production and social relations under the medieval Arab-Islamic caliphate, the general tendency among Marxist researchers is to regard feudal relations as dominant.
They disagree, however, about the specific historical form that this feudalism took.
The reason for this disagreement lies in the complex overlap between two sets of features.
The first were feudal features inherited from the social systems that existed in the conquered regions before the Arab-Islamic conquests, especially the Persian and Byzantine systems.

The second were new forms of production relations created by the Islamic system of landholding. This system itself changed repeatedly through new interpretations and practical measures, beginning with the land policy of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb during the early conquests and continuing into the ninth century CE.
These newer relations were marked, first, by several different forms of landownership and, second, by the use of both slave labour and free peasant labour on the land.
The complicated interaction of all these historical features made it difficult for researchers to identify the true character of the dominant economic and social system.

It also made possible conclusions such as the claim that Arab-Islamic society developed directly from a patriarchal tribal society—the society of the Jāhiliyya—into a feudal society, without first passing through slavery as a complete, developed and dominant social system.
According to this view, “slavery also existed in tribal, pre-Islamic society, but only as a phenomenon contained within the broader social and economic structure of that society.”
Some Soviet thinkers speak of both European feudal society and Arab feudal society, while stressing that feudalism in Europe differed from feudalism in the East.
They describe the difference in roughly the following way.

After the collapse of the centralized Roman Empire, Europe broke up into competing principalities. These fought one another as smaller political units were gradually brought together around larger feudal powers.

Out of these conflicts came the process through which larger national communities were formed. This process continued throughout the Middle Ages and did not reach its final stage until the nineteenth century.

The Vatican served as a major centre of authority in Europe and eventually became a state exercising power over the different European feudal forces, while retaining its specifically Christian religious character.
In the East, by contrast—as in Russia—there was no dominant church organized as a religious state existing alongside a separate civil state.

Instead, there was a vast Arab state controlling enormous parts of the East and holding them together under a single political authority. This made it possible for the economy and the sciences to develop.
While the Church in the West sought to maintain its authority over the feudal lords, everything in the East was subject to the caliph. The head of state often held absolute power.
Yet the caliph’s authority was not primarily theological. It was civil and political.

Unlike Western feudal lords, who were bound by religious authority and by their relationship with the pope, the caliph was rarely subject to religion in an absolute sense. More often, religion itself was made subject to his political authority and to the interests of the state.
This account helps clarify some of the main political differences between Arab-Islamic society and European society.
But it does not explain the basic features of the mode of production in either one.
So the real difference remains unclear.
To identify it properly, we first need to know what kind of production relations existed before the Arab-Islamic conquest in the countries that later became part of the caliphate.
Then we need to understand how those relations changed after the caliphate was established and a new society emerged under its rule.
Most of the conquered countries had previously belonged either to the Byzantine social and economic system or to the Persian Sasanian system.
We therefore need to know the particular features of each.
Recent Soviet historical literature contains several attempts to answer this question.
One appears in the large Soviet encyclopedic work History of the World, which presents two theories about the Byzantine system.
